Inter-run agreement and reliability

Source: R/agreement.R
agent_agreement.Rd

[consistency()] answers whether an agent is stable across repeated runs with a single disagreement rate, and [score_confidence()] puts an interval on a single run's per-slice score. Neither answers the reliability question a reviewer actually asks: how much do the repeated runs agree beyond what chance alone would produce? A system that passes four fifths of its cases on every run looks stable by raw agreement even when the agreeing verdicts are no better than coin flips. This reports the chance-corrected agreement that tells the two apart.

It treats each repeat in the run as a rater and each case as a subject rated once per repeat, with the grader's verdict ("pass", "fail", "warn", "na") as the nominal category. On that balanced, fully-crossed design it computes three established statistics and a per-case breakdown. Nothing here calls a model or the network; the verdicts are read from the run as it stands, so every figure is reproducible from the run alone.

Usage

agent_agreement(run)

Arguments

run

An `r4agent_run` with `repeats` greater than one. Every case must have been run the same number of times, which [run_benchmark()] guarantees.

Value

An object of class `r4agent_agreement`: a list with `percent_agreement` (the overall mean pairwise agreement), `kappa`, `kappa_method` ("Cohen's kappa" or "Fleiss' kappa"), `strength` (the Landis & Koch label, or `NA` when kappa is `NA`), `expected_agreement` (\(p_e\)), `n_items`, `n_runs`, `categories` (the verdict levels seen), and `by_item`, a data frame with one row per case (`id`, `slice`, `severity`, `n_runs`, `distinct` verdicts, `modal` verdict and per-case `agreement`) ordered with the least-agreeing cases first.

Details

The statistics are textbook nominal-agreement measures; no weight, threshold or scoring rule is invented here.

Overall percent agreement is the mean across cases of the per-case pairwise agreement \(P_i\), the proportion of rater pairs that assigned case \(i\) to the same category. With \(m\) repeats and \(n_{ij}\) repeats placing case \(i\) in category \(j\), $$P_i = \frac{1}{m(m-1)} \left( \sum_j n_{ij}^2 - m \right),$$ the per-subject agreement of Fleiss (1971). For two repeats this is simply the fraction of cases that returned the same verdict both times.

Cohen's kappa is reported when there are exactly two repeats (Cohen, 1960). With observed agreement \(p_o\) (the share of cases whose two verdicts match) and expected agreement \(p_e = \sum_j p_{1j} p_{2j}\) formed from each repeat's own category marginals \(p_{1j}, p_{2j}\), $$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}.$$

Fleiss' kappa is reported for three or more repeats (Fleiss, 1971). With mean observed agreement \(\bar P = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i P_i\) and expected agreement \(\bar P_e = \sum_j p_j^2\) from the pooled category proportions \(p_j = \frac{1}{nm}\sum_i n_{ij}\), $$\kappa = \frac{\bar P - \bar P_e}{1 - \bar P_e}.$$ Fleiss' form treats the repeats as interchangeable, which is what repeated runs of one agent are; Cohen's form, used for two, keeps each repeat's marginals separate. When every verdict falls in one category the expected agreement is 1, kappa is \(0/0\) and is returned as `NA`: with no variation to correct for, a chance-corrected statistic has nothing to say.

The `strength` label follows the rule of thumb of Landis & Koch (1977) (< 0 "poor", 0–0.20 "slight", 0.21–0.40 "fair", 0.41–0.60 "moderate", 0.61–0.80 "substantial", 0.81–1 "almost perfect"). It is their published guideline, quoted for orientation only; this package enforces no kappa threshold and the label changes no score and no verdict.

References

Cohen, J. (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 20(1), 37–46.

Fleiss, J. L. (1971). Measuring nominal scale agreement among many raters. Psychological Bulletin, 76(5), 378–382.

Landis, J. R. & Koch, G. G. (1977). The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data. Biometrics, 33(1), 159–174.

See also

[consistency()], [consistency_strata()], [score_confidence()]

Examples

suite <- agent_suite(list(
  agent_case("steady", "ping", "ok", slice = "stable", grader = "contains"),
  agent_case("flaky", "toggle", "ok", slice = "shaky", severity = "high",
             grader = "contains")
))
# A deterministic offline runner that flips one case's answer every other call.
seen <- new.env()
flip <- function(x) {
  n <- if (exists(x, seen, inherits = FALSE)) get(x, seen) else 0L
  assign(x, n + 1L, seen)
  if (x == "toggle" && (n + 1L) %% 2L == 0L) "no" else "ok"
}
run <- run_benchmark(suite, flip, repeats = 4L, quiet = TRUE)
ag <- agent_agreement(run)
ag
#> 
#> ── Inter-run agreement: 2 cases over 4 runs ────────────────────────────────────
#> Categories seen: "fail" and "pass"
#> Percent agreement: 0.6667 (mean pairwise)
#> Fleiss' kappa: 0.1111 (slight), expected 0.6250
#> 
#> ── Cases where runs disagree most 
#> flaky (shaky, high) agreement 0.3333, 2 verdicts
#> 
#> Strength label follows Landis & Koch (1977); it changes no score or verdict.
ag$by_item
#>       id  slice severity n_runs distinct modal agreement
#> 1  flaky  shaky     high      4        2  fail    0.3333
#> 2 steady stable   medium      4        1  pass    1.0000
